strengths: The orientation-resolved analysis reveals structured successes and failures that average accuracy obscures. These findings have an identifiable audience in visual robustness, representation learning, and computational neuroscience.

The experiments provide substantial descriptive evidence: three object categories, multiple seed-orientation ranges, five repetitions, and a fixed training-image budget. Additional architectures, pretraining, augmentation, and reduced-data controls strengthen the empirical contribution, although their coverage varies.

The geometric model offers an interpretable description of generalization patterns through small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related components. Component ablations help explain differences between experimental conditions.

The learning paradigm and main behavioral findings are communicated clearly through illustrative heatmaps and an explicit training/test distinction. Links to code and generated data support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Necessary: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Figures 5b–c establish associations between activation statistics and accuracy, but do not establish that shared-feature invariance is transferred from fully-seen to partially-seen instances or causally enables recognition. Shared image geometry and differences between experimental conditions remain alternative explanations. Sections 3.3–4 should consistently present dissemination and the biological analogy as hypotheses, or provide targeted interventions or controls that distinguish these explanations.

Necessary: The generalizable/non-generalizable partition requires clarification and validation. Section 2.5 thresholds f_w at 10% of its maximum, but Equation 4 sums four sigmoid outputs and is fitted using Pearson correlation, which does not calibrate its offset or scale as accuracy. Figure S9c displays scores around 1.8–2.4, which would all exceed the stated threshold because f_w cannot exceed 4. Specify any missing normalization and demonstrate robustness to reasonable thresholds. This ambiguity directly affects Figures 5, S6, and S8.

Necessary: The invariance metric does not establish invariance across individual orientations. Equation 6 compares region-averaged activations; strongly view-selective responses can have identical regional means and receive maximal invariance. Equation 7 additionally retains only pairs whose two means exceed the activity threshold, potentially comparing different selected populations across conditions. Validate the interpretation using orientation-level response variation, report the retained counts L, and assess threshold sensitivity, or restrict the claims to similarity of regional mean responses.

Necessary: Distinguish fitted description from independent prediction. Sections 2.4 and 3.2 optimize Pearson correlation and report that same statistic without describing a held-out evaluation for the geometric model. The reported correlations support a compact fit to measured behavior, but do not establish predictive performance on unseen conditions. Either evaluate fixed fitted parameters on suitable held-out data or narrow the predictive claims accordingly.

Necessary for the cross-category diversity interpretation: Increasing fully-seen instances from 10 to 40 also reduces partially-seen target instances from 40 to 10. Category-conditioned guessing therefore increases from 2.5% to 10%; the fixed 10% reference in Figure S8 is not applicable throughout this sweep. Correct these baselines and distinguish improved orientation transfer from changes in the target-class composition, using a fixed target set or appropriately qualified conclusions.

Optional: Enlarge the labels in the dense quantitative figures and report numerical correlations with uncertainty for the neural analyses, preferably separated by experimental condition. These changes would make the evidence easier to assess. Broader real-image or model evaluations would extend the findings but are not prerequisites for a properly scoped empirical contribution.
